t.1.27.1: Śaunaka said: What was the offense of great Indra, and what his negligence, O son of a Sūta? How was Garuḍa born through the austerity of the Vālakhilyas?
t.1.27.2: How indeed was the king of birds the son of Kaśyapa, a twice-born one? And how did he become unassailable and unslayable by all beings?
t.1.27.3: And how did that sky-roamer come to move wherever he wished and to possess strength at his own will? This I wish to hear, if it is recited in the Purāṇa.
t.1.27.4: What you are asking me about is a subject of the Purāṇa. Listen, O twice-born one, as I tell you all of it in brief.
t.1.27.5: When Kaśyapa, the Prajāpati, desiring a son, was performing a sacrifice, the ṛṣis, the gods and the gandharvas gave him their help, so it is said.
t.1.27.6: There Śakra was appointed by Kaśyapa to the task of bringing the firewood, and so too were the sages, the Vālakhilyas, and the other hosts of deities.
t.1.27.7: But Śakra, the mighty lord, lifted up a load of firewood befitting his strength, resembling a mountain, and brought it as if without great difficulty.
t.1.27.8: Then he saw on the path some tiny seers, no bigger than the middle joint of a thumb, who were together carrying a single palāśa leaf-stalk.
t.1.27.10: And Puraṃdara, possessed by pride and intoxicated with his own might, laughed at all of them, stepped over them, and, treating them with contempt, swiftly passed them by.
t.1.27.11: Then they, filled with rage and with their fury exceedingly aroused, undertook a great work at that time, one that would strike fear into Śakra.
t.1.27.9: He saw those ascetics rich in austerity, who seemed shrunk into their own limbs, fasting and feeble in strength, struggling in a cow's hoofprint filled with water.
t.1.27.12: Those brahmins of great austerity made offerings, according to rule, into Jātavedas with mantras high and low; hear with what desire they did so.
t.1.27.14: "By the fruit of our austerity, let there be born today a fearsome one, a hundredfold greater than Indra in heroism and in valor, swift as thought."
t.1.27.13: Firm in their vows, they intended: "Let there arise another Indra of all the gods, mighty at will, going wherever he wishes, a bringer of fear to the king of the gods."
t.1.27.15: Learning of that, Śatakratu, king of the gods, sorely distressed, went there for refuge to Kaśyapa of rigorous vows.
t.1.27.16: Having heard that from the king of the gods, Kaśyapa the Prajāpati then approached the Vālakhilyas and asked them about the success of their rite.
t.1.27.17: And those speakers of truth replied to him, "So be it." Then Kaśyapa, the Prajāpati, spoke these words to them, beginning with conciliation.
t.1.27.18: This one has been made Indra in the three worlds by the command of Brahmā, and you too, O ascetics rich in austerity, are striving for the sake of an Indra.
t.1.27.20: Let this one, exceedingly strong and mighty, be the Indra of the birds; and let favour be shown to the king of the gods, who is entreating you.
t.1.27.19: O best of the virtuous, you should not make the word of Brahman false; and it is not my wish that this resolve of yours be made false.
t.1.27.21: Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, the Vālakhilyas, rich in austerities, paid homage to the Prajāpati, the best of sages, and replied.
t.1.27.23: So let this fruitful deed be accepted by you; and in this matter, act just as you see what is best.
t.1.27.22: O Prajāpati, this undertaking of all of us is for the sake of an Indra; and this undertaking, aimed at offspring, is desired by you as well.
t.1.27.24: At that very time, the goddess Vinatā, the beautiful daughter of Dakṣa, auspicious and illustrious, was longing for a son.
t.1.27.25: Having practised austerities, devoted to her vows and pure, having bathed at the time of the puṃsavana rite, she approached her husband; then Kaśyapa spoke to her.
t.1.27.26: O queen, this undertaking you desire shall bear fruit: you will give birth to two heroic sons, lords of the three worlds.
t.1.27.27: Through the austerity of the Vālakhilyas and likewise through my own resolve, two illustrious sons will be born to you, born of that resolve and honored by the worlds.
t.1.27.28: And the blessed Mārīca spoke to her once again: "Let this embryo, destined for very great prosperity, be carried with vigilance."
t.1.27.29: Alone he shall exercise the lordship of all winged creatures, a hero honored by the world, a sky-goer of strength as great as he wills.
t.1.27.30: Then Prajāpati, being pleased, said to Śatakratu: "These two birds will be your brothers, your companions."
t.1.27.31: Through these two no harm shall come to you, Puraṃdara. Let your distress depart, Śakra; you alone shall be Indra.
t.1.27.33: Thus addressed, Indra went to heaven, free from apprehension; and Vinatā too, her purpose accomplished, was then joyful.
t.1.27.32: Never again must you insult the expounders of the Veda in this way, nor should they be scorned out of your pride, for they are exceedingly wrathful and their words are poison.
t.1.27.34: She gave birth to two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa; of the two, Aruṇa was deformed, and he became the forerunner of the sun.
t.1.27.35: But Garuḍa was consecrated as the Indra of the birds, the lord of the winged ones. Let this very great deed of his be heard, O delight of the Bhṛgus.
